source: CARE Cambodia (Pailin), "TIP Training on Maize Production" / បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្ដបច្ចេកវិទ្យា ផលិតកម្មដំណំពូតក្របម, 2009. Funded by AusAID (ACIMA project), the European Union (Pailin Food Security Program), and ACIAR (CCPMP project).
text:
Good land preparation plays a major role in successful corn production. Ploughing has two main purposes: it makes the soil fine, loose, and level, and it reduces early weed growth. However, ploughing also has downsides: it causes the soil to lose moisture, which is a significant problem especially at the start of the early wet-season planting window; and ploughing does not reliably kill weeds outright — it can actually cause more weeds to emerge, by spreading weed seeds and exposing weed roots to light and air.

Recommended ploughing practices: plough soil that has adequate moisture, but not soil that is too wet, since wet soil is difficult to plough and becomes compacted; on sloped land, plough along contour lines running across the slope (not up and down it) to reduce runoff and erosion; plough at a steady, moderate speed rather than too fast; and aim for soil that is fine and level, which is especially important when using a machine (seeder) for planting.

For land planted to corn twice a year, farmers commonly burn crop residue before ploughing, aiming to reduce pests, disease, and weeds, and to make land preparation easier. Recent research cited in the source indicates that leaving/keeping crop residue in the field does not, in itself, naturally increase disease pressure. However, before burning residue, farmers should consider the effect on nitrogen and potassium loss: nitrogen in the soil is easily lost through runoff, erosion, and volatilization from heat, while potassium contained in the crop residue itself is lost when that residue is burned. Corn residue also serves important functions if left on or incorporated into the field: it acts as ground cover that protects against erosion, helps retain soil fertility and moisture, and eventually decomposes into fertilizer for the next crop.
